hook: The exiled poet of Florence who imagined a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Heaven.

pages.x: Dante was born in Florence in 1265. At nine he saw Beatrice Portinari, a girl of eight, and fell in love at first sight. He met her again nine years later, when she greeted him in the street, and he wrote about her for the rest of his life.

Beatrice married someone else and died at 24. Dante was heartbroken, and told the story of his love in poems and prose, The New Life. He married Gemma Donati, chosen for him when he was a boy, and had four children, but never wrote a word about her.

He went into politics and fought as a cavalryman. In 1302, while he was away on a mission to the pope, his rivals took over Florence and sentenced him to be burned alive if he ever came back. He never saw his city again.

In exile he wrote The Divine Comedy, an epic journey through Hell, Purgatory and Heaven. Guided by the Roman poet Virgil and then by Beatrice, Dante meets the dead, from popes to his own enemies. Over the gate of Hell are the words: "Abandon all hope, you who enter here."

Dante filled Hell with real people: crooked politicians boiling in tar, a pope stuck head first in a hole with his feet on fire, and a place waiting for Pope Boniface VIII, who was still alive. Readers loved spotting who was where.

Instead of Latin, the language of scholars, he wrote in the Tuscan spoken in the streets, so ordinary people could read him. His poem made the speech of Florence the basis of modern Italian, and he is called the father of the Italian language.

He died of malaria in Ravenna in 1321, just after finishing the poem. Florence later demanded his bones back; the monks of Ravenna hid them in a wall, where they were found in 1865. Florence still has an empty tomb for him.
The Divine Comedy is one of the greatest poems ever written, and it made Tuscan the language of Italy. Its pictures of Hell still shape how people imagine the afterlife.
pts: The father of the Italian language
Gave the world its picture of Hell
